title: Linear Inequalities
intro: Inequalities describe ranges of solutions rather than single values, and the SAT tests them in algebra and in word problems about limits and constraints. This chapter covers solving inequalities, compound inequalities, interval notation and number-line representation. Read each topic, try the problems with the hint ladder, then take the 8-question topic test.

items.name: Flip rule
items.formula: multiplying or dividing by a negative reverses the inequality

topics.name: Solving Inequalities
topics.details: Solving a linear inequality uses the same balance moves as an equation, with one crucial rule: when you multiply or divide both sides by a negative number, you must reverse the inequality sign. So −2x < 6 becomes x > −3 after dividing by −2. Adding or subtracting never flips the sign. The solution is a range of values, often written with an inequality symbol. Checking a test value from your solution range in the original inequality confirms the direction. This single flip rule is the most common SAT slip in inequality questions.

solved.solution: Divide by −2 and flip the sign: x > −3.

hints: Dividing by a negative flips the sign.

topics.name: Compound Inequalities
topics.details: A compound inequality combines two conditions. An "and" inequality like −3 ≤ 2x − 1 < 5 means both hold at once; solve by doing the same operation to all three parts, giving a bounded range such as −1 ≤ x < 3. An "or" inequality is satisfied when either part holds and usually gives two separate rays. For "and" problems keep the variable in the middle and isolate it by adding then dividing across all parts. The SAT uses compound inequalities for "between" situations and for combining constraints in word problems.

solved.solution: Add 1 to all parts: −2 ≤ 2x < 6; divide by 2: −1 ≤ x < 3.

topics.name: Interval Notation
topics.details: Interval notation is a compact way to write a solution range. Parentheses ( ) mean an endpoint is excluded (strict < or >); square brackets [ ] mean it is included (≤ or ≥). So x > 2 is (2, ∞), and −1 ≤ x < 3 is [−1, 3). Infinity always takes a parenthesis because it is never reached. The smaller number is written first. Converting between inequalities, number lines and interval notation is a quick SAT skill: match each ≤/≥ to a bracket and each </> to a parenthesis.

unsolved.problem: Write the interval (−∞, 5] as an inequality.

topics.name: Number Line Representation
topics.details: A number line pictures an inequality's solution set. Use an open circle at the endpoint for a strict inequality (< or >) and a closed (filled) circle for an inclusive one (≤ or ≥), then shade in the direction of the solutions — right for greater-than, left for less-than. A compound "and" inequality is shown as a shaded segment between two circles. Reading these correctly is essential: the type of circle tells you ≤ versus <, and the shading direction tells you which way the solution runs. The SAT often asks you to match an inequality to its graph.

solved.problem: How is x > 3 shown on a number line?
solved.solution: An open circle at 3 with shading to the right.
A closed circle at −1 with shading to the left.

solved.problem: What inequality has a closed circle at 2 shaded right?
solved.solution: Closed circle means inclusive; shaded right means greater: x ≥ 2.
Open circle at −2, closed circle at 3, shaded between them.

unsolved.problem: How is x < 5 shown on a number line?
What inequality has an open circle at −4 shaded right?
What inequality has a closed circle at 6 shaded left?

unsolved.answer: Closed circle at 1, open circle at 4, shaded between.
